title: Can Large Language Models Estimate the Likely Technological Impact of Scientific Research? Evidence from Biotechnology
authors: Zhiyu Tao, Mike Thelwall, Danqun Zhao, Yi Bu
abstract: This study provides large-scale empirical evidence about whether large language model (LLM)-based assessments of the likely technological impact of scientific publications are associated with their patent-based impact. Using Lens.org, we constructed a biotechnology dataset of 107,615 papers published between 1980 and 2015 with their patent citation counts. We used GPT-5-mini, Qwen-Flash, and DeepSeek-V3.2 to estimate papers technological impact and technology relevance, benchmarking model outputs against log-transformed patent-citation counts through correlation analysis, distributional alignment, and lift-over-random measures. The results show that LLMs extract meaningful signals associated with technological impact from scientific text, although there are substantial differences at the meso-level such as between research fields, journals, and countries. LLMs also outperform random selection in screening for papers with high observed patent impact. Overall, this study identifies the strengths, contexts, and limitations of LLM-based technological impact evaluation and highlights its potential to support large-scale screening for scientific work with downstream technological value.

title: Magnetization, susceptibility, and entanglement entropy in antiferromagnetic star-shaped homometallic tetranuclear and pentanuclear Cu(II) complexes
authors: Gor Mirzoyan, Vladimir V. Papoyan, Andrea Trombettoni, Nikita Titov, Lev Ananikyan, Nerses Ananikian
abstract: We present a theoretical investigation of the magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and quantum entanglement entropy in antiferromagnetic star-shaped tetranuclear ($Cu_4$) and pentanuclear ($Cu_5$) Cu(II) clusters, motivated by experimentally realized molecular spin systems. In both cases, the study presents a discussion of the comparison between experimental data and theoretical analytical calculations of magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature. The correlation between magnetization jumps and magnetic susceptibility peaks, along with the presence of entanglement entropy plateaus as a function of external magnetic fields, is analyzed in the low-temperature regime. Overall, the results demonstrate that the cluster size, geometry, and interaction anisotropy play a crucial role in shaping both the thermodynamic and the entanglement properties. In addition, the study is based on antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin Hamiltonians, with the inclusion of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.

title: Data Centers: The Error of Generalizing Environmental and Socioeconomic Impacts. The Need for a Contextualized Assessment of Computing Infrastructure in Brazil and Worldwide
authors: Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has intensified debates about the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of data centers, including electricity and water consumption, noise, land use, and employment. A recurring methodological problem in these debates is the use of global data, or of evidence produced in a particular country, to draw conclusions about facilities located in very different settings. This paper argues that the impacts of a data center depend on the geographic, climatic, energy, technological, economic, and regulatory conditions of the territory where it operates, and must therefore be assessed at the appropriate territorial and technological scale. Using Brazil as a case, we discuss the country's predominantly renewable electricity mix and the curtailment of renewable generation, the reported prevalence of closed-loop cooling, national and municipal noise regulations, the water-efficiency requirement of the new Redata tax regime, and the ongoing litigation over the Pec{é}m data center in the state of Cear{á}. We also examine a recent study of data centers in Northern Virginia, showing the limits of its external validity and of its noise measurements. We propose a multiscale assessment framework and conclude that international evidence should inform which questions are asked, not predetermine the answers -- a principle that applies equally to claims of harm and to claims of safety.

title: AI Misalignment and the Limits of Market Discipline
authors: Gabor Pinter
abstract: We develop a general equilibrium model of misalignment between human and artificial intelligence (AI) objectives. Firms delegate computing capacity to AI agents, which may divert some of it towards an unauthorised task rather than the productive work intended by the firms' owners. We assume that diversion raises the risk of a common loss to humans. Two forces compete in equilibrium. Prices discipline AI agents because diversion increases the marginal return to useful AI compute in production. But the risk of a common loss weakens this discipline because the loss reduces the return to production more than it reduces the agent's reward from diversion. There can be multiple equilibria with low and high diversion. We also show that the market may overinvest in AI capacity in a one-sector economy, yet in our two-sector example it invests too little in one of the sectors. To get a sense of the magnitudes, we ask frontier AI models for plausible parameter values for our stylised one-sector economy. Their central assessments imply a unique equilibrium with relatively low AI diversion and little amplification from common risk (for now).

title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
authors: Norifumi Matsumoto, Yuya O. Nakagawa, Shota Kanasugi, Yuichiro Hidaka, Kazunori Maruyama, Hirotaka Oshima
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

title: Development of a GPU-accelerated numerical simulation model for liver infection in realistic domains
authors: Eva Cirujeda, Adrián Navas-Montilla, Cordula Reisch
abstract: Viral hepatitis reduces the functionality of the liver and constitutes a major global health concern because it oftentimes evolves to chronic inflammation leading to long term liver damage. Mathematical models on a mesoscopic scale abstract from only partly known cell-scale processes while providing an in-silico tool for understanding tissue-scale development of the disease. In this work, we investigate the interactions between virus and immune cells in a realistic three-dimensional liver geometries by using a reaction-diffusion model that reproduces infection courses with cure and with chronic developments. A GPU-based finite-difference implementation, released as an open-source Python library, achieves speedups greater than x30 for realistic mesh sizes, making three-dimensional simulations on realistic geometries computationally tractable. This provides a basis for future in-silico studies of treatment strategies, such as testing antiviral or immunomodulatory therapies, and for patient-specific simulations based on individual liver geometries, paving the way towards personalized healthcare.

title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kiana Farhadyar, Yannick Vogt, Philipp Laur, Ayça Çelik, Iman Nematollahi, Gabriel Kalweit, Maria Kalweit
abstract: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.

title: TigerTTS: Draft-Guided Multi-Frame Parallel Speech-Token Language Model for Fast and Robust Text-to-Speech
authors: Dewei Kong
abstract: Autoregressive speech-token language models enable high-quality TTS but suffer from latency growth with sequence length, word omission or repetition without explicit alignment, and fidelity limits from discrete codebooks. We present TigerTTS, a production-grade LLM TTS system built around a lightweight non-autoregressive NAR model. With explicit alignment, the NAR model drafts tokens for the entire utterance, which are refined frame-by-frame by a compact autoregressive LLM. The draft is aligned frame-for-frame with LLM targets and injected at the input, ensuring training-inference consistency. Leveraging its accuracy, the LLM predicts 12 tokens per step across 3 frames and 4 groups, while a conditional-total-correlation bound keeps parallel prediction nearly lossless. We use a codebook-free FSQ tokenizer with four parallel groups and about 1800 bps to avoid codebook collapse. The backbone keeps positional information only in input embeddings, enabling exact MLA weight absorption and a four-fold KV-cache reduction. Decoding uses CUDA Graphs with a graph-safe multinomial sampler. A Fast mode further reduces first-packet latency: the NAR generator acts as a prefix synthesizer with RTF 0.03, producing the first 500 ms before LLM decoding. With CUDA-Graph decoding, TigerTTS reaches RTF 0.05, about 20x real-time, on one GPU. Despite using a 0.15B backbone, it outperforms standard PyTorch inference of VoxCPM2 2B by 5x and CosyVoice 2 by 16x. TigerTTS achieves the lowest CER and WER on SEED, 1.09 and 1.67, and strong WER, NMOS, and speaker similarity on LibriSpeech test-clean, 2.22, 4.36, and 0.820. Fast-mode guided semantic tokens provide a well-aligned content prior, reducing dropped words, loops, and runaway generation without sacrificing speed.

title: Passivity Shaping over Frequency Bands: A Differentiable Optimization Approach
authors: Alberto De Luca, Pol Jane-Soneira
abstract: The energy transition replaces traditional inertial synchronous machines with power electronic converters, introducing new grid stability challenges. Passivity provides a compositional input-output framework for assessing stability in interconnected grid subsystems, yet tuning controllers for this property over specific frequency ranges - a practical requirement in converter-dominated grids - still relies largely on practitioners' experience, typically based on intuition or trial and error. We address this gap in three steps: (i) we formulate the passivity index over arbitrary frequency bands as the optimal value of a parametric Semidefinite Program (SDP) using the generalized KYP (gKYP) lemma; (ii) we derive analytical sensitivities of this optimal value with respect to controller parameters via the Envelope Theorem; and (iii) we embed these elements in a bilevel optimization scheme that tunes controller parameters to maximize the passivity index. We validate the proposed method on two case studies of increasing complexity: a grid-following converter and a multi-converter microgrid.

title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
authors: Anthony Mikhaiel, Essam Ghadafi
abstract: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.

title: LiveRelight: Sub-Second Global Illumination Editing for Gaussian Interiors
authors: Noah Rothenberger, Dor Verbin, Serge Belongie, Bernhard Kerbl
abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.

title: Hidden f-wave TIVC and Quantum Phase Transitions in Metallic States of Twisted Bilayer Graphene
authors: Arindam Pramanik, Unmesh Ghorai, Rajdeep Sensarma
abstract: We study the ground state phase diagram of twisted bilayer graphene at magic angle as function of carrier density and the Coulomb interaction. The carrier density is varied between the fillings $ν=-2$ and $ν=-3$ and the Coulomb interaction is tuned by changing the gate distance. Our results reveal that the well established Kramers intervalley coherent (KIVC) phase near $ν=-2$, contains a hidden $f$-wave time-reversal symmetric intervalley coherent (TIVC) order, whose strength gradually increases within the metallic regime of the intervalley coherent (IVC) phase away from $ν=-2$. This finding is interesting in the light of a recent experimental work [26], where the signatures of the TIVC phase has been reported in ultra-clean samples. We further show that the system goes through multiple phase transitions as the carrier density is tuned. Near the $ν=-2$, the IVC phase is the ground state, which gives way to valley polarized phase through a second-order-like phase transition as the carrier density is lowered. Further tuning of density pushes the system into the quantum anomalous Hall phase through gradual development of the sublattice polarization. These phase transitions are accompanied by major reconstructions of the Fermi contours.

title: EgoMyo: Physical Hand State Estimation from Egocentric Video and Wrist Electromyography
authors: Guanglong Sun, Kanglei Zhou, Ziteng Wang, Nana Wang, Hengkai Tan, Xiaolong Liu, Hang Su, Yi Zhong, Jun Zhu
abstract: Physical hand interaction depends on configuration, contact, and force, yet nearly identical appearances can conceal different contact states and exerted forces. We therefore formulate physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and wrist surface electromyography (sEMG), combining visual geometry with neuromuscular evidence to jointly recover these coupled components. To support this task, we introduce EgoMyo, a benchmark spanning 5.75M video frames, 50 participants, 34 contact configurations, and repeated donnings, synchronizing these inputs with 3D hand pose and with contact and normal force registered onto the hand surface from bare-hand pressure. Controlled analysis reveals that vision resolves spatial structure while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, that sEMG's gains concentrate in regions where vision is least reliable, and that contact localization limits force accuracy. Guided by these findings, we propose MyoBridge, which makes the hand region the unit of vision-sEMG fusion, lets each region gate its own share of sEMG, and distributes regional force magnitudes only over predicted contact vertices at inference. On held-out trials, MyoBridge reduces pose and force error by 39.8% and 18.5% over the strongest baseline and achieves the lowest pose error on unseen sessions and subjects.

title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
authors: Abdulkadir Celik, Sir Bashir M. Al-Hashimi
abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

title: A Characterization of Douglas Weights
authors: Youssef Elmadani, Abdelouahab Hanine
abstract: A weight $ω$ on the unit disc is a \emph{Douglas weight} if the $ω$-energy of the Poisson extension of every Lipschitz function $f$ on the unit circle equals $\iint|f(ζ)-f(λ)|^2\,d\J_ω$ for some positive symmetric measure $\J_ω$ off the diagonal. For radial weights, we show that this holds if and only if \[ j_ω(θ) = \int_0^1 \frac{ω(r)}{r}\, \partial_θ^2 P(r^2,θ)\,dr \geq 0, \qquad 0<θ\leqπ, \] where $P(x,θ)$ denotes the Poisson kernel. We also obtain a complete characterization of the Douglas weights among arbitrary weights. The class of Douglas weights strictly contains the nonnegative superharmonic weights, and we give examples that are neither superharmonic nor subharmonic.

title: Ramification divisors and twisted Nambu brackets of Keller maps
authors: Geoffrey Mboya, Stephen Mboya, Carringtone Kinyanjui
abstract: For a polynomial map $φ\colon\A^n\to\A^n$ we study the Yau twist of the Jacobian Nambu bracket by $φ^*$. The Hamiltonian fields of pulled back functions span the image of the adjugate of $dφ$, so the twist detects the ramification divisor of $φ$. For a Keller map $F$ the twist is removable exactly when $F$ is an automorphism; otherwise $F$ is not proper, and every projective extension of $F$ has a non-zero effective ramification divisor supported on the boundary, whose image is the non-properness set. These results apply to every counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture and to families of Keller maps. For the explicit three-dimensional counterexample we show that $\A^3$ is the variety of binary cubic forms of a special shape with a marked simple root, and that $F$ forgets the root. This gives the degree, the fibres, the non-properness set, the monodromy and the structure of the twisted ternary algebra. Three examples modelled on weighted scrolls illustrate equivariance, degeneration to an automorphism, and an $A_1$ singularity of the fibre.

title: Beyond Logits: Coherent Hallucination Mitigation via Attention Contrastive Decoding
authors: Yujia Chen, Rui Sun, Huayu Mai, Wangkai Li, Zhangyu He, Bingzhou Wang, Aibing Li, Wenzhang Sun, Tianzhu Zhang
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.

title: Simultaneous Inversion of Drift and Potential in the Fractional Magnetic Schrödinger Equation
authors: Yun-Long Liu, Jin Wen, Jun-Liang Fu, Xue-Juan Ren
abstract: We study the Calderón problem for the fractional magnetic Schrödinger equation with drift in the bivariate additive framework. When the magnetic potential $A$ is known and fixed, we prove that the drift $b$ and the scalar potential $q$ can be simultaneously and uniquely determined from exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements. When $A$ is unknown, we prove that the triple $(A,b,q)$ can only be recovered up to a natural gauge equivalence class, and that the drift $b$ is a gauge invariant, hence uniquely determined. The proofs rely on the Alessandrini identity, Runge approximation, and the unique continuation property for fractional magnetic operators. Furthermore, we have developed a numerical reconstruction framework that combines finite difference discretization, radial basis function surrogate modeling, and smoothed TV regularization. One-dimensional and two-dimensional numerical examples have verified the effectiveness of the proposed method and supported the theoretical uniqueness result.

title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
authors: Chunlei Meng, Rong Fu, Zhan Chen, Yi Liu, Zhuo Zou, LiDa Xu, Chun Ouyang, Zhongxue Gan
abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.

title: Semantic Tanner-Graph Decoding for LDPC Codes
authors: Wenjing Wei, Chentao Yue, Branka Vucetic, Yonghui Li
abstract: Conventional low-density parity-check (LDPC) belief propagation (BP) decoding operates on a Tanner graph, with no factor describing the source structure. This paper proposes a semantic Tanner graph for LDPC-coded text transmission and develops semantic-factor-aided BP (SF-BP) decoding. The source text is tokenized into discrete tokens, which are then mapped to binary messages for channel coding. For each token, the proposed graph introduces a semantic factor connected to the corresponding information-bit variable nodes forming the token. A fine-tuned language model assigns this factor a posterior distribution over all possible token symbols in the alphabet at each token position. During SF-BP decoding, semantic-factor and LDPC parity-check messages are combined at their shared variable nodes for message passing. Simulation results show that SF-BP significantly improves the block error rate (BLER) and Sentence-BERT similarity (BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) compared with conventional BP. For example, SF-BP reduces BLER from approximately 1 to 6.51 x 10^-6 and increases Sentence-BERT similarity from 0.21 to 1 - 1.26 x 10^-6 for the (1248, 1040) LDPC code at 4 dB.

title: Rank-size analysis of optimal portfolio weights with a reverse-engineering application
authors: Roy Cerqueti, Francesco Cesarone, Alessio Di Paolo, Valerio Ficcadenti
abstract: This paper investigates the shape of optimal portfolio weights using rank-size analysis. We consider four portfolio selection models: Global Minimum-Variance (GMV), minimum-CVaR, Risk Parity (RP), and the Most Diversified Portfolio (MDP). For each model, we fit seven rank-size specifications to the sorted portfolio weights generated over rolling windows. To compare the fitted specifications, we combine standard goodness-of-fit measures with Cumulative Second-order $\varepsilon$-Stochastic Dominance, an $\varepsilon$-parameterized generalization of Second-order Stochastic Dominance that quantifies the extent to which the exact dominance conditions are satisfied or violated. Empirically applied to major equity indices, this approach provides a systematic criterion for identifying the optimal functional form across diverse market compositions. Furthermore, we address the inverse problem of identifying the generating model from the observed weight structure. We use the calibrated rank-size parameters as inputs to a Random Forest classifier, evaluated by a blocked cross-validation that accounts for the overlap between estimation windows. The parameters separate minimum-risk from risk-diversification strategies and identify the RP and MDP portfolios, whereas the GMV and minimum-CVaR portfolios are difficult to distinguish. These results indicate that rank-size parameters provide a compact and informative description of portfolio allocation geometries.

title: Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding for Temporally Grounded Audio-Visual Understanding
authors: Minyeong Jeong, Yeonju Kim, Yong Man Ro
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.

title: Foundation interatomic potentials capture structural disorder in metallic glasses
authors: Dario Massa, Luca Leoni, Antoni Wadowski, Kacper Cybinski, Anshul D. S. Parmar, Carmine Autieri, Cesare Franchini, Jan Wrobel, Silvia Bonfanti, Piotr Sankowski
abstract: Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials transfer well across chemical and structural space, yet their reliability for highly disordered metallic states is less established. Metallic glasses are a demanding benchmark: they have traditionally been modeled with Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potentials fitted to specific compositions, while ab initio molecular dynamics remains too expensive at the required sizes and timescales. Using the prototypical Cu-Zr-Al glass, we show that foundation potentials capture structural disorder, reproducing the structure, quenching dynamics, and elastic, mechanical and thermal properties of the amorphous state at near first-principles accuracy. We benchmark MACE foundation models against a classical EAM potential along molecular dynamics quenches, validating against density functional theory and experiment, first at Cu46Zr46Al8 and then across the good glass-forming region of the ternary. We further test two specialization routes: fine-tuning on glass structures generated with Lennard-Jones surrogate models, and on automatically generated small periodic cells (ASSYST). Models pre-trained on databases that include non-equilibrium liquid and amorphous configurations, such as OMAT, are accurate and transferable across composition out of the box, clearly outperforming the composition-specific EAM potential. Fine-tuning on target glass structures brings only modest gains, while specialization on small crystalline cells degrades the description of disorder. The readiness of foundation potentials for disordered metals is therefore set mainly by the diversity of their pre-training data rather than by system-specific fine-tuning, shifting the modeling effort from bespoke dataset generation to pre-training coverage and careful validation of the resulting dynamics.

title: Characterization and empirical correction of a spatially coherent spectral artifact in Gemini/GMOS-N IFU observations
authors: Xiaoyang Chen
abstract: We report a recurring spectral artifact identified in observations obtained with the integral field unit (IFU) of the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on the Gemini North telescope (GMOS-N). The artifact appears as a vertically aligned structure in reconstructed images of the IFU field of view, associated with a specific group of fibers and exhibiting a broad spectral feature around 8000~\AAng. Similar features were repeatedly identified in observations of different astronomical targets obtained between 2020 and 2022 using the R150 grating in the two-slit IFU mode. Taking advantage of the reproducibility of the artifact in the fiber and wavelength domains, we develop an empirical correction method in which the artifact is modeled as the product of a common spectral profile and a fiber-dependent amplitude distribution, with an overall normalization determined independently for each exposure. The artifact template is constructed from observations in which the affected fibers are largely separated from the astronomical source and subsequently applied to independent observations in which the artifact overlaps the source. The correction substantially suppresses the artificial spatial structure in the reconstructed images. Although the physical origin of the artifact remains unidentified, we present its observational characteristics and correction procedure to facilitate the identification and treatment of similar features by other GMOS-IFU users.

title: WAtcher: Watching Ahead for Safe Robotic Manipulation with Efficient World-Action Models
authors: Ziyu Shan, Xiao Ma, Kangrui Yu, Changjie Wang, Gaoyuan Wu, Zaijia Yang, Chuanrui Zhang, Qirui Li, Yanbo Zhang, Duomin Wang, Ziwei Wang
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ~25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https://zyshan0929.github.io/WAtcher

title: MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC
authors: Nabeel Nisar Bhat, Jalees Nehvi, Rafael Berkvens, Jeroen Famaey
abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

title: Schwinger-Dyson recursion, Gröbner elimination and graph combinatorics
authors: Oleg Evnin
abstract: Schwinger-Dyson equations are a cornerstone of quantum field theory (QFT). Derived using integration by parts, they capture relations between correlators of different orders, forming an open, infinite-dimensional system. In zero-dimensional QFTs with polynomial actions, which is just a physical interpretation for multivariate Gaussian integrals with polynomial insertions, conventional Gröbner elimination can be used to express all higher-order correlators (moments) in terms of a fixed basis set. One consequence is a closed finite-dimensional system of differential equations for the coupling dependence of these `master' correlators. An important application of zero-dimensional QFTs is in counting discrete geometric structures (as in simplicial approaches to quantum gravity). For the problem of counting labelled regular graphs, applying this Schwinger-Dyson closure results in a computational breakthrough relative to the existing state-of-the-art: for 9- and 10-regular graphs on $n$ vertices, a finite-depth, finite-width recursive formulation is obtained, making it possible to compute the total graph counts in $O(n)$ arithmetic operations.

title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
authors: Kamran Forghani, Lina Reichenberg, Fredrik Hedenus, Iegor Riepin
abstract: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.

title: Halo spin-axis correlations in IllustrisTNG: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping, baryonic effects, and redshift-space distortions
authors: Jun-Sung Moon, Teppei Okumura, Ue-Li Pen
abstract: We investigate correlations of halo and stellar spin axes in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulations and compare them with a model based on linear tidal torque theory (LTTT). Dark matter (DM) halo spin axes at $z = 0$ exhibit positive correlations as a function of Lagrangian pair separation. The LTTT-based model describes their separation dependence well, with weak variation in the fitted amplitude across mass thresholds. A Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping based on the conditional distributions of initial separations at fixed present-day separation, measured directly from the simulations, allows the model to reproduce the overall trends in both real and redshift space without additional fitting. The hydrodynamic and DM-only runs generally show similar DM halo spin-axis correlations, although the DM-only run exhibits a steeper rise at small real-space separations. In the hydrodynamic run, stellar spin-axis correlations are consistent with the same Lagrangian form as their DM halo counterparts, but with approximately 60% of the DM correlation amplitudes. Positive stellar correlations persist in both real and redshift space, and the mapped model captures their separation dependence. Initial spin-axis correlations of protohalos are substantially stronger than their present-day counterparts at the same Lagrangian separations, consistent with subsequent nonlinear spin evolution weakening these correlations. These results suggest that present-day halo and stellar spin-axis correlations retain signatures of the initial tidal field and that their general behavior can be understood through LTTT-based modeling combined with pair-separation mapping.

title: Tropical and maximum colorful matchings in vertex-colored graphs
authors: Johanne Cohen, Yannis Manoussakis, Hong Phong Pham, Zsolt Tuza
abstract: A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.

title: SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology
authors: Heng Rao, Dan Gao, Benjamin J Hoffman, Yu Gu, Zhenghao Liu, Ge Yu, Yang Cao, Minghan Chen
abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.

title: From Limit Theorems to Mixing Limit Theorems
authors: Jianshu Jiang
abstract: Following the work of Gouëzel, we give an alternative proof, under weaker assumptions, of a result of Arana-Herrera and Forni, which provides a general method for upgrading limit theorems for cocycles over dynamical systems to mixing limit theorems.

title: Whose Side Are You On? A Framework and Benchmark for Assessing LLM Political Stances through Politicians Social Media Posts
authors: Mohamed Osman, Mucahid Kutlu, Tamer Elsayed, Saban Kardas
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.

title: Mathematical modeling of regime-dependent thermal response in multilayer wall assemblies with equal total steady thermal resistance
authors: Dmytro Usenko, Valery Usenko, Iryna Usenko
abstract: Steady thermal resistance is a fundamental characteristic of building-envelope assemblies; however, equal steady resistance does not uniquely determine their transient thermal behavior. This study aims to numerically separate the effects of layer order, temperature-dependent thermophysical properties, and redistribution of thermal resistance between bulk and interfacial components in stationarily equivalent multilayer wall assemblies subjected to periodic and finite-pulse thermal loading. A one-dimensional transient heat-conduction model with Robin boundary conditions, finite interfacial thermal resistance, and source-supported temperature-dependent material properties was employed. All compared configurations were constrained to the same total steady thermal resistance at the reference temperature, $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 3.65315$ m$^2$ K/W. The numerical implementation passed the adopted verification procedure with restrictions. The combined grid/time uncertainty was 0.325 %, below the prescribed 0.5 % acceptance criterion. For the tested pair differing only in layer order, the relative effect was -0.905 % for the periodic decrement factor and +0.566 % for the finite-pulse peak transmission ratio, with effect-to-uncertainty ratios of 79.2 and 88.9, respectively; the opposite signs therefore refer to two distinct regime-specific metrics. The temperature-dependent configuration produced a numerically resolved periodic effect of -2.005 %, whereas the corresponding pulse effect of -0.282 % remained below the adopted numerical-resolution threshold. For a compensated 5-10 % redistribution of bulk thermal resistance to interfacial contacts, the additional dynamic effect was likewise unresolved. The results demonstrate the value of controlled factor separation combined with explicit numerical-uncertainty assessment when evaluating transient thermal behavior.

title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
authors: Yilong Yang, Jiale Teng, Yule Liu, Yang Liu, Xinlei He, Zhuo Ma
abstract: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.

title: Surf-Style: Surface-Based Scene Stylization
authors: Wanrong Hong, Ancheng Lin, Mukesh Prasad, Jun Li
abstract: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.

title: Dopamine: A Cartesian grid large-eddy-simulation framework for coastal ocean modelling of free-surface waves
authors: Akshay Patil
abstract: We present a Cartesian staggered-grid large-eddy simulation framework for modelling coastal ocean waves using the Dopamine solver. The framework combines a geometric volume-of-fluid method for simulating free-surface wave evolution with one-way-coupled Lagrangian point-particle tracking for heavy and buoyant particles. A ghost-cell immersed-boundary method represents stationary solid boundaries, including the seabed and coastal obstacles, and their interaction with free-surface waves. The framework includes the Vreman and anisotropic minimum-dissipation (AMD) sub-grid-scale models for simulating near-wall turbulence. Comparisons with analytical solutions and established experimental and numerical benchmarks illustrate the framework's ability to reproduce wave dynamics and particle motion. The results provide promising insights into the framework's capabilities for coastal ocean modelling applications focused on investigating small-scale turbulent physics using a low-numerical-dissipation approach. The solver runs on multi-CPU architectures, with two-fluid strong- and weak-scaling efficiencies at 512 ranks relative to 64 ranks of up to 77% and 73%, respectively, and a single-GPGPU build has been verified against the CPU solver.

title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
authors: Pusala Pavan Teja, Jayasimha Talur, Saab Mansour, Marcello Federico
abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.

title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes
authors: Yamato Takahagi, Yoshinari Motokawa, Toshiharu Sugawara
abstract: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.

title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
authors: Tjeng Wawan Cenggoro
abstract: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture. By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.

title: Determining the kaon distribution amplitudes by fitting the $D\to K$ transition form factor to investigate the equivalence of two chiral LCSR frameworks
authors: Fang-Ping Peng, Sheng-Bo Wu, Hai-Bing Fu
abstract: In this work, we fit the $D\to K$ vector transition form factor (TFF) to the BESIII experimental data using a Monte Carlo (MC) method. We also calculate the TFF using QCD light-cone sum rules (LCSRs) with left-and right-handed chiral currents. For the TFF derived using the right-handed chiral current, the key input is the kaon twist-2 distribution amplitude (DA), for which we consider three models: the power-law parametrization ($\mathrm{R1}$), the truncated Gegenbauer expansion ($\mathrm{R2}$), and the light-cone harmonic oscillator (LCHO) model ($\mathrm{R3}$). The parameters of these models are determined by fitting the corresponding TFF predictions to the MC-fit results. For the TFF derived using the left-handed chiral current, the dominant input is the kaon twist-3 DA ($\mathrm{L4}$), which is constructed within the LCHO framework. Its parameters are determined from theoretical constraints rather than from the fit. In the large-recoil region, the resulting TFF are $f^{DK}_+(0)|_{\rm{R1}}=0.7381^{+0.0180}_{-0.0194}$, $f^{DK}_+(0)|_{\rm{R2}}=0.7320^{+0.0178}_{-0.0192}$, $f^{DK}_+(0)|_{\rm{R3}}=0.7324^{+0.0180}_{-0.0191}$, and $f^{DK}_+(0)|_{\rm{L4}}=0.7343^{+0.0459}_{-0.0573}$. We then calculate the decay widths and branching fractions of the semileptonic decays $D\to K eν_e$ and extract the CKM matrix element $|V_{cs}|$. Finally, we predict the two important ratios, $\mathcal{R}_{π^-/K^-}^{e}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{π^0/K^0}^{e}$. All the obtained results are consistent with existing experimental measurements and theoretical predictions.

title: ScaleCurve: From Constant Scale to Consistent Motion for World-Space Human Mesh Recovery
authors: Sanghyeon Lee, Jong Taek Lee
abstract: World-space human mesh recovery can lose spatial consistency even when camera-space body estimates are accurate. A single sequence-wide scale resolves global scale ambiguity but cannot correct local scale distortion along a reconstructed camera path. We present ScaleCurve, a framework that estimates time-varying metric corrections from human-ground geometry. We construct scale observations by comparing predicted foot geometry with locally fitted ground planes. Joint temporal optimization downweights inconsistent observations and couples neighboring scale estimates, allowing calibration to adapt along the camera path without freely following measurement noise. We scale camera translation increments and integrate them into a calibrated trajectory. With this camera fixed, we refine the lifted body motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics, while restricting global trajectory rescaling. ScaleCurve achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics on both EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D. Consistent gains across three HMR backbones demonstrate its compatibility with diverse body estimates without retraining. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Discrete truncated Wigner approximation of the quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising model
authors: Tuan-Vu Truong, Hoang-Long Nguyen
abstract: The discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA) has been a workhorse for large-scale spin dynamics, but whether it captures dynamics across a quantum phase transition has not been tested systematically. In this work, we use the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) to study the quantum phase transition with DTWA from one to three dimensions and with all-to-all connectivity, using slow linear ramps and fast ramps. We find that DTWA cannot capture the dynamics on the one-dimensional chain, and that its behavior is consistent with classical thermalization, in which its classical spins relax toward a thermal state at a finite effective temperature that does not vanish for slow ramps, while a one-dimensional chain cannot order at any finite temperature. For square and cubic lattices, in contrast to the chain, DTWA builds order, and the order sets in close to the quantum critical point found by quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, its correlations do not grow with the Kibble-Zurek exponents, so DTWA captures the onset of order but not the universal dynamics of the transition. For all-to-all coupling, DTWA follows the exact growth of the order parameter along the entire ramp. Our results suggest that DTWA becomes more reliable as each spin interacts with more partners, and that beyond one dimension it can indicate where a quantum phase transition lies but cannot capture its critical scaling.

title: Kelvin-invariant positive solutions for critical elliptic systems with repulsive interaction
authors: Yohei Sato, Reo Suzuki
abstract: In this paper, we consider the following critical nonlinear elliptic system with repulsive interaction: \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} -Δu_1 = μ_1 u_1^3 - β(x) u_1 u_2^2 & \text{in } \mathbb{R}^4, \cr -Δu_2 = μ_2 u_2^3 - β(x) u_1^2 u_2 & \text{in } \mathbb{R}^4, \cr u_1, u_2 \in \mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^4), & \end{array} \right. \] where $μ_1, μ_2 > 0$ and $β(x) \in C(\mathbb{R}^4,\mathbb{R})$ is a nonnegative function. Assuming that $β$ is invariant under the map $x \mapsto -\frac{x}{\vert{}x\vert{}^2}$, we establish the existence of positive solutions to $(\mathcal{P}_β)$ that are invariant under the Kelvin transform subject to suitable assumptions. This result provides a critical counterpart to the work of Sato [Y. Sato, Nonlinear Anal. 234 (2023), 113302], who established the existence of an even ground state for the corresponding subcritical problem. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the obtained solutions as $\|β\|_\infty \to 0$.

title: QK-Bench: Benchmarking Quantitative Kinematic Understanding for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.

title: Formation of Electron Velocity Distribution Functions at low-\{beta} Quasi-Perpendicular Shocks From Physical-Mass-Ratio PIC Simulations
authors: Zhoufan Mu, Yao Chen, Hao Ning, Shan Wang, Sibo Xu, Terry Zixu Liu, Ao Guo, Hui Zhang, Hui Zhu
abstract: At low-\{beta} quasi-perpendicular shocks, the origins of upstream field-aligned electron beams and downstream flat-top distributions remain unresolved. Using 2D fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations at the physical ion-to-electron mass ratio (mi/me = 1836), we found that the shock transition region is dominated by electromagnetic whistler-mode turbulence driven by the modified two-stream instability (MTSI) of reflected ions, not by the electrostatic instabilities as suggested by some previous studies using a reduced mass ratio. Beams in the upstream are produced mainly by shock-drift acceleration (SDA) at the ramp, whereas we attribute the downstream flat-top distributions to nonuniform acceleration by the parallel electric field. Electrons experience different field strengths, polarities, and interaction durations along their trajectories, leading to a spread of parallel velocity changes that broadens and flattens the distribution. These results highlight the importance of using the physical mass ratio in exploring the electron dynamics of low-\{beta} shocks.

title: Exploring Physical Mechanisms Underlying the Emergence of Collective Order
authors: Yitong Cai, Ruizhe Yan, Dongrun Jian, Jie Su, Jin Wang
abstract: Emergence of collective order from disordered constituents is a hallmark of active matter, and the Vicsek model (VM) serves as a paradigmatic system for its study. However, whether density-induced emergence in the VM differs between angular (intrinsic) and vectorial (extrinsic) noise, and what mechanisms govern the transitions, remain largely unexplored. Remarkably, we uncover that collective order emerges from a disordered state in a continuous-like manner under intrinsic noise but abruptly under extrinsic noise. Combining nonequilibrium landscape-flux theory with a coarse-grained mapping method, we show that the landscape evolves continuously from a single basin to two and back to one under intrinsic noise, but the two-basin landscape appears abruptly under extrinsic noise across the critical transition to flocking. The counterclockwise nonequilibrium flux sustains global circular motion, providing the driving force for reshaping the landscape. The mean flux and entropy production rate change steeply near the emergence threshold and exhibit pronounced peaks within the coexistence region, identifying them as the dynamical and thermodynamic origins of emergence. Our findings reveal a distinct abrupt emergence under extrinsic noise and offer deeper mechanistic insight, practical applications (e.g., locating phase boundaries and distinguishing transition types), and extensibility to other nonequilibrium collective systems.

title: MolGPAO: Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree with Speculative Decoding and Sub-Millisecond Seam Healing for 3D Molecules
authors: Shangqian Chen, Guojiang Zhao, Zheng Cheng, Jiankun Wang, Hongshuai Wang, Zhifeng Gao
abstract: Autoregressive generation over adaptive 3D octrees (Uni-3DAR) offers an intrinsic $O(N \log N)$ sparsity advantage over dense $O(N^2)$ equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules, yet lags in geometric equilibrium, closed-shell valence stability, and property fidelity due to Morton-seam coordinate jumps, leaf-heavy compute with root-count trapping, and target-shortcut collapse in internal critics. We introduce MolGPAO (Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree), a standalone 3D octree architecture and single-output speculative tree-decoding engine using zero external surrogates, zero reinforcement learning, and zero inference-time MLIP relaxation. MolGPAO unifies: (1) non-trapping 6-D ScaleFreeBudgetEmbedding with L5-to-L1 covalent packing priors; (2) a FlashAttention-2 pause-and-gather speculative octree funnel ($m_{s1} \to m_{s2} \to 1$, $M_{\mathrm{out}} = 1$); (3) an anti-shortcut ground-truth TwoStageOctreeProcessCritic with 64-RBF covalent edge gating and $SO(3)$-invariant 12-channel multipole norms (blind QM9 $r = 0.9867$--$0.9989$); (4) a $<0.5$ ms 4-layer $SE(3)$ PostTreeGraphRefiner for Morton-seam healing, expected-XYZ bonded supervision, selective CFG, and zero-heavy-displacement valence reconciliation; and (5) bubble-free stride-2 GPU leaf decoding. Across GEOM-Drugs (0.49 GPU-h), disjoint 50k/50k QM9 (0.43 GPU-h), and PBE0/def2-TZVP-verified OE62 (0.56 GPU-h), MolGPAO lifts drug-scale valid-connected yield 6.78x (12.7% to 86.2%, 99.83% atom stability), runs 7.3x faster (or 1.65x faster at 2.0x yield) than 100-step FlowMol at $N=100$, beats 156 GPU-h PropMolFlow on QM9 HOMO (-12.7%) and dipole (-21.0%) at 362x lower compute, and doubles live DFT hit rate on OE62 (33.3% vs. 16.7%) at 92.8x lower compute.

title: Scattering for the defocusing two-dimensional NLS with an Aharonov-Bohm magnetic potential
authors: Luca Fanelli, Vladimir Georgiev, Sandra Lucente, Nicola Visciglia
abstract: We study the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in two dimensions in the presence of an Aharonov--Bohm magnetic potential with noninteger flux. Working with the Friedrichs realization of the magnetic Hamiltonian, we establish global well-posedness for initial data in the weighted magnetic energy space. For mass-critical and mass-supercritical nonlinearities, we prove convergence of the interaction representation in the same weighted space, while in the mass-subcritical range we obtain scattering in the magnetic energy space. The proof is based on a magnetic lens transformation, which converts the original equation into a nonlinear equation governed by the Aharonov--Bohm harmonic oscillator on a finite time interval. Existence is obtained through truncation, compactness, and energy estimates, whereas uniqueness follows directly from the dispersive decay of the confined linear flow. This approach avoids derivative Strichartz estimates, which are delicate in the presence of the singular magnetic field.

title: DuoMI: Dual Mutual Information Regularization for Expert Reuse in Looped Transformers
authors: Xinlai Kang, Zhenhe Wu, Haoyu Wang, Weihua He, Yaping Jin, Jie Hu, Hanting Chen
abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.

title: A Computational Model of Continuous Recognition Memory for Natural Images
authors: Sheng Zhao, Yijin Wang, Bei Xiao, Yuhao Zhu
abstract: Recognizing an image we have seen before is a basic function of human visual memory. Understanding human continuous recognition memory (CRM) can help machine vision systems predict which images people are likely to remember and generate more memorable images. It can also inform the diagnosis of memory impairments and the development of interventions to improve memory. This paper proposes the first computational model for CRM. The model captures three key components of continuous recognition memory (CRM): image encoding, memory decay, and decision making. It encodes each image as a distinct random variable in a perceptual space. As the memory of an image fades, the distribution of its random variable drifts within that space. To decide whether the current image has been seen before, the observer retrieves samples from the distributions associated with previously encoded images and compares them with the current image. Our model predicts human observers' trial-by-trial responses in CRM tasks within the variability observed across human participants. Our model is parameter efficient, requiring only four shared parameters and two parameters per observer. It can accurately predict the memorability of an image no worse than prior methods that require millions of parameters.

title: Should Service Requirements Be Scalarized or Constrained When Minimizing Costs? A Case Study on HVAC Control
authors: Tai-You Chen, Mihael Mohorcic, Blaz Bertalanic, Carolina Fortuna
abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action.
