In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.

title: Empirical De-Quantization and Norm-Controlled Spectral Audit of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning in an Emerging Equity Market
authors: Pavel Chuklanov
abstract: Quantum-inspired machine learning in econophysics describes states of financial markets through matrix Hamiltonians, using ground-state expectations to predict returns and spectral gaps to identify crises. Although early work reports encouraging advances, it remains unclear whether these stem from genuine noncommutative quantum geometry or from conventional classical regularization and scale effects. We test this in a controlled audit of matrix-form Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) and variational quantum circuits on the Moscow Exchange (2020-2025), combining daily equity data with causally lagged macro news under realistic trading costs, short-selling bans, and abrupt shifts in market regimes. By using capacity-matched operator swaps -- which progressively eliminate complex Berry phases and matrix noncommutativity down to a commuting classical Gibbs radial-basis limit under scale-invariant regularization -- as well as testing spectral indicators against radial-norm null hypotheses and untrained GUE random matrices, we isolate the contribution of each quantum element. In out-of-sample data, neither complex phases, noncommutativity, nor circuit entanglement improves the ranking of returns relative to classical controls. Once feature magnitudes are normalized, apparent crisis detection from raw spectral gaps drops below chance levels. These results show that on noisy equity panels, matrix-form QCML acts as an adaptive spectrally bounded classical smoothing kernel: it reliably integrates lagged news and curbs extreme crisis forecasts without passing economic multiple-testing thresholds, while our audit provides operator-swap and random-matrix controls for evaluating future quantum-inspired financial models.

title: Phonon-Aware Electron-to-Nuclear Spin Quantum Memory in NV Centers
authors: Manjith Baby Sarojam Chellam
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits. In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center. The model includes the NV electron spin, a coupled 13C nuclear spin, the hyperfine interaction, an effective microwave/radio-frequency-assisted SWAP interaction for writing and reading, a single effective phonon mode with longitudinal spin-phonon coupling, and Lindblad relaxation and dephasing channels. The dynamics are simulated with the Lindblad master equation in QuTiP, using the secular approximation and a hyperfine-resonant drive in the rotating frame. Without spin-phonon coupling and electron decoherence, the write-store-read protocol recovers the stored state with a fidelity above 0.9999. With the default decoherence rates, increasing the spin-phonon coupling from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers the worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, and the fidelity oscillates with the phonon-mode period because electron-phonon entanglement generated during the write step is partially undone during the read step. With a phenomenological temperature-dependent rate model, the fidelity decreases monotonically from 0.9997 at 1 K to 0.9938 at 300 K, while storage-time losses follow the assumed nuclear-spin decoherence rates. The storage-time plots, temperature sweep, and parameter maps identify operating regimes for NV-center quantum memory, and the accompanying open-source code provides a reproducible framework for studying phonon-limited quantum memory.

title: Towards 360$^\circ$ Embodied UAV Tracking Without Turning
authors: Bingyu Li, Wu Du, Zhiyuan Zhao, Junyu Gao, Xuelong Li
abstract: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $π_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $π_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/

title: Transport Layer-Driven Optimization of Color and Efficiency in TADF OLEDs for Large-Area Applications
authors: Manish Kumar, Jawid Nikan, Luiz Pereira
abstract: Balancing structural simplicity with high efficiency is crucial for practical applications of organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), especially in large-area lighting devices. Optimizing the charge-transport layers in multilayer OLEDs controls the recombination zone within the emissive layer, thereby enhancing the device's performance. Herein, we experimentally and computationally investigate how the thicknesses of the electron and hole transport layers affect the performance of orange-red thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) OLEDs. Using a TADF emitter, 2-[4-(diphenylamino)phenyl]-10,10-dioxide-9H-thioxanthen-9-one (TXO-TPA), at 10 wt\% concentration in 4,4-Bis(N-carbazolyl)-1,1-biphenyl (CBP) host, we achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency ($η_{EQE}$) of 20.86\% and a peak luminance of 32,800 cd m$^{-2}$. Using a combination of drift-diffusion and optical simulations, we reveal how variations in hole- and electron-transport-layer thicknesses modulate the charge-carrier balance and shift the recombination zone within the emissive layer. This tuning not only optimizes exciton formation but also enables color tuning from green to red without altering the emissive material. Our findings highlight the critical role of transport layer engineering in achieving efficient, color-controlled OLEDs with simplified architectures. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrate a large-area OLED device (~20 cm$^{2}$), achieving an impressive $η_{EQE}$ of 17\%, underscoring the scalability and practicality of our approach for general lighting applications.

title: Near Optimal Pure Stepsize Adaptation Acceleration for Gradient Descent on Nonconvex Optimization
authors: Yin Liu, Ziyang Zeng, Junyu Zhang
abstract: Existing accelerated first-order methods for nonconvex optimization typically rely on momentum or extrapolation, requiring auxiliary vectors beyond the current iterate and gradient. On the other hand, memory-free stepsize scheduling alone can accelerate certain convex problems, while no guarantee exists for nonconvex problems. This paper closes this gap by proposing Nonconvex Adaptively Clipped Chebyshev (NACC) gradient descent method, which achieves near optimal acceleration while keeping the vanilla gradient descent update. NACC combines an adaptive selection of reversed fractal Chebyshev stepsizes with an epoch-wise clipping mechanism to control the aggressiveness of stepsizes. For nonconvex problems with Lipschitz continuous gradients and Hessians, we establish a near-optimal $\widetilde O(ε^{-7/4})$ complexity. If the problem is convex in addition, then, without modification, NACC automatically achieves an $\widetilde O(ε^{-3/4})$ accelerated complexity. Importantly, NACC guarantees the standard quadratic sufficient descent at every iteration, even when the stepsizes are substantially larger than the conventional choice. These monotonicity properties further facilitate practical implementations that adaptively adjust the estimated gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants, demonstrating significant advantages in numerical tests against the existing nonconvex acceleration benchmarks.

title: Revisiting the Schottky-Mott Relation for Metal/ Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Interfaces: The Role of Interface Dipoles
authors: Chih-Piao Chuu, Shu-Jui Chang, Yu-Miin Sheu, Zih-Syuan Huang, Wei-Tung Liu, Po-Wei Chen, Sui-An Chou, Yu-Tung Lin, Chih-I Wu, Wen-Hao Chang, Chun-Liang Lin, H. -S. Philip Wong, Iuliana P. Radu
abstract: High contact resistance, predominantly stemming from Fermi-level pinning (FLP), becomes a critical bottleneck in the contact engineering of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) based two-dimensional field-effect transistors (2DFETs). Our study re-examines the inherent nature of FLP in 2D semiconductors, particularly focusing on regimes where the material thickness is commensurate with the interface thickness. Through the synergistic application of first-principles calculations and experimental validation via ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), we rigorously establish the metal effective work function (eWF) as the definitive figure of merit for substantiating the Schottky-Mott relation. Our findings indicate that FLP is intrinsically governed by both long-range dipole interactions and extended short-range Lennard-Jones potentials. This framework, in conjunction with the linear Schottky-Mott relation, improves predictive capabilities in contact engineering.

title: Almost Tight Hardness of Approximation for $0$-Extension
authors: Qingyun Chen, Weihao Zhu
abstract: In the $0$-Extension problem, we are given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, a collection $T \subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals, and a metric $D$ over terminals $T$. The goal is to find a retraction $f:V\rightarrow T$ that maps every terminal to itself, while minimizing the sum over all edges of the product of the edge's weight and the distance in $D$ between the terminals to which its endpoints are assigned, i.e., \[ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{\{u,v\}} \cdot D(f(u), f(v)). \] Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar achieve the best known approximation ratio of $O(\log k / \log \log k)$, while the known approximation hardness is $Ω(\sqrt{\log k})$ assuming the unique games conjecture. In this work, we establish an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ hardness of approximation for every constant $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and arbitrarily large fixed $k$, almost matching the upper bound in the exponent of $\log k$. The main technical contribution is an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation. Our construction is inspired by randomized extensions of expanders introduced by Schwartz and Tur for the metric relaxation. The result then follows from an existing theorem by Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz that translates the integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation to the approximation hardness for every fixed $k$.

title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
authors: Junda Ying, Xinyu Wang, Peijie Zhou, Lei Zhang
abstract: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.

title: Event-WAM: Learning to Act with Event-Derived Futures
authors: Jongseong Bae, Hyunwoo Kim, Yeongin Lee, Eubin So, Ha Young Kim
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage future visual modeling for robotic action learning, with recent studies exploring alternative or complementary objectives beyond conventional RGB prediction. We introduce Event-WAM, which incorporates event-derived visual changes as auxiliary future supervision alongside RGB. Event-WAM constructs temporally structured event representations from RGB demonstrations and encodes them using a frozen pretrained RGB video VAE, without training an event-specific VAE. Joint RGB--Event latent flow matching provides appearance- and change-oriented supervision without requiring event observations or explicit future generation at inference. Across simulated benchmarks, Event-WAM maintains comparable performance under standard conditions, while robustness gains under perturbations are benchmark-dependent, including improvements on LIBERO-Plus. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate improved manipulation success under both standard and unseen perturbation conditions. Further analyses show that policy improvements are not consistently accompanied by higher future prediction fidelity, suggesting the potential of change-oriented supervision for action learning.

title: CoTAMP: Cooperative Task and Motion Planning for Quadruped Robots with Large Language Models
authors: Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
abstract: Some environments cannot be traversed by a single quadruped robot, for example a ledge that one robot can climb only from its partner's back or a gap that must be bridged with boxes. Solving them requires cooperative task and motion planning (TAMP). Previous works are limited to the motions of a single robot or only select actions from a predefined set of skills. We propose a framework with two parts: task planning that invents motions not defined in advance, and motion generation that realizes the invented motions. Both parts consist of large language model (LLM)-based modules and code-based modules. Task planning divides the trajectory of the whole task into steps and fixes the robot poses at the step boundaries. Motion generation produces keyframes that describe the motion of each step and turns them into a continuous trajectory through kinematic synthesis. The code-based modules check every plan and motion and return failures to the LLM-based modules for correction. The whole trajectory is then refined by trajectory optimization to satisfy the dynamics. On three simulated courses with two RAIBO2 robot models, our framework produced kinematically valid references in all 30 trials, all of which converged in trajectory optimization. Compared with several baselines, our framework showed advantages in success rate, dynamic feasibility, execution time, and generation time and cost. Project page: https://woojin8098.github.io/CoTAMP/

title: A Sweedler dual seen as a terminal object in a category of bialgebras
authors: Lo{ï}c Foissy
abstract: We study the Sweedler dual of the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{K}[X]$ equipped with the multiplicative coproduct $δ(X) = X \otimes X$, and show that the resulting bialgebra $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$ is the terminal object in the category of pairs $(B, λ)$, where $B$ is a bialgebra and $λ$ is a character of $B$. This generalizes a result of Aguiar, Bergeron, and Sottile on combinatorial Hopf algebras in the graded and connected setting. We describe the subcoalgebras and subbialgebras of $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$, which lead to the introduction of the spectrum of a bialgebra. We also study the particular cases double bialgebras (bialgebras equipped with two compatible coproducts), firstly examining their connection to unital near-semirings or near-rings. Introducing a subbialgebra of $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$ obtained from the intersection with another Sweedler dual, we prove it is the terminal object in the category of double bialgebras. As a consequence, we show that the spectrum of any double Hopf algebra is a subgroup of the group of roots of unity. This imply that not any bialgebra can become double. We finally apply this framework to a bialgebra of graphs with a coproduct given by contraction and deletion of edges, relating its invariants to Bergman colorations of edges arising from graphical matroids.

title: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control
authors: Soyeong Oh
abstract: Learning hypothesis weights from informative auxiliary data can improve the power of multiple testing. Even when the weights are learned independently of the tests, the validity of weighted Benjamini-Hochberg depends on their joint distribution. We use reference observations to certify a sufficient dependence condition for one-sided Gaussian tests. An intersection-union test of uncertain correlation signs determines whether to apply weighted Benjamini-Hochberg or a prespecified fallback at an adjusted level. Under conditional separation of certification and testing, the procedure controls the false discovery rate (FDR) for every Gaussian correlation matrix satisfying the stated sampling assumptions and weight constraints. We establish a boundary obstruction to uniform certification and matching minimax sample-size bounds for worst-case pair sets and the all-pairs problem. In the parameter ranges of the matching bounds, the minimax sample size grows logarithmically with the number of checked pairs and quadratically with the inverse of their positive margin. For homogeneous Gaussian observations with known marginal variances, residual contrasts from the testing subjects provide an independent source of certification scores. Simulations with up to 4,950 checked pairs, comparisons under a common subject budget, and Gaussian designs based on correlations estimated from the Healthy Brain Network illustrate the trade-off between certification and detection power.

title: The Gradient Difference Induced by Detaching the Denominator in QK Normalization
authors: Yuanqi Zhang, Haocheng Wang, Congping Lin
abstract: QK normalization divides each query and key by its own RMS norm before the attention scores are computed. Treating this denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the parameter gradients. We derive a closed form for the difference between the gradient under this detached rule and the gradient under the standard rule. For a single token, this difference is parallel to the token's own query; it changes only the query norm and has no first-order effect after normalization. The queries, however, are computed by a projection matrix $W_Q$ shared across all tokens. The gradient difference on $W_Q$ therefore equals $W_Q$ right-multiplied by a weighted second moment of the inputs, and it decomposes exactly into three components: a radial component that changes only the norm of $W_Q$, a tangential component that changes the query directions of other tokens, and an upstream component that changes the gradient passed to earlier layers. Under AdamW, the radial component drives $W_Q$ to a larger equilibrium norm and reduces its angular update per step. Paired experiments on a small Transformer language model are consistent with this analysis. Detaching the query denominator consistently raises the test loss, and the gap persists across hardware, evaluation datasets and learning rates. All three components remain non-negligible throughout training, with the tangential component the largest. Norm growth and the smaller angular update appear only on the detached projection matrix, while the other projection matrix is essentially unchanged. With a learnable scale, however, we observe no resolvable loss gap.

title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
authors: Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng
abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

title: Integration of Vision-Language-Action Control for Autonomous Forklift Unloading with Limited Real-World Data
authors: Koshi Oishi, Seigo Ito
abstract: Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making. Recently, vision--language--action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts. Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored. Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data. Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets. As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost. We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8% of the collected forklift data by duration. The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants. The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data.

title: Parallel sums of nilpotent elements: exact realization and structured eigenvalue splitting
authors: Yaashaa Golovanov
abstract: We prove that, over every infinite field and for $m\ge2$, the parallel sums $N(N+C)^{-1}C$ of nilpotent $m\times m$ inputs with invertible sum are exactly the matrices of nullity at least two. Every positive split of the target nullity between the input kernels is realizable. Over $\mathbb{C}$, we determine the paired derivative image and characterize universal full matrix cancellation at nonzero residues. For analytic input paths, nilpotence is required only at the base. An adjugate identity forces the last two characteristic coefficients to be $O(\varepsilon^2)$, yielding sharp bounds $O(|\varepsilon|^{2/3})$ at nonzero three-dimensional nilpotent residues and $O(|\varepsilon|^{1/(m-2)})$ at nilpotent residues for $m\ge4$. At every base with residue of type $[m-1,1]$, $m\ge4$, we prove a generic splitting law, also with fixed input sum. For $m\ge5$, it has $m-2$ roots on the scale $|\varepsilon|^{1/(m-2)}$ and two on the scale $|\varepsilon|^{1/2}$, separating the largest-root and spectral-gap scales. A separate sharpness family keeps both inputs nilpotent and two roots zero. At the nonzero nilpotent three-dimensional boundary, a finite coefficient criterion computes the splitting orders for each exceptional affine fixed-sum direction. For each such path, the punctured spectral gap is at least $c|\varepsilon|^3$ near zero for some $c>0$, and the exponent is optimal over this class. Over a nonzero unital ring with $2$ invertible, we construct two $3\times3$ matrix inputs, each of nilpotency index exactly three, with invertible sum. In the complex unital Banach case, the residue has spectrum ${0}\cup\tfrac12σ(Q)$ for every coefficient $Q$. With the common core allowed to vary, a complex matrix is a finite-Drazin Hua output if and only if its nullity is not one.

title: X-Matte: VAE-Free Pixel-Space Flow Matching for Single-Step Image Matting
authors: Zanyi Wang, Jiaang Li, Dengyang Jiang, Ziru Wang, Chengzu Li, Davit Abrahamyan, Harry Yang, Serge Belongie, Mengmeng Wang
abstract: Pre-trained generative models offer rich visual priors for image matting, but their adaptation often relies on variational autoencoders (VAEs), whose spatial compression can degrade fine alpha details and introduce additional inference overhead. To address these limitations, we propose X-Matte, a VAE-free pixel-space flow matching framework for single-step image matting. By eliminating latent compression, X-Matte formulates the RGB-to-alpha transition as a continuous flow directly in pixel space. We adopt trajectory-wide x-prediction with transition-aware alpha supervision, enabling the model to learn from intermediate states while directly predicting the target alpha matte in a single forward pass. This design avoids both VAE encoding and decoding and iterative sampling. Extensive experiments demonstrate performance competitive with state-of-the-art trimap-free matting methods on P3M benchmarks, together with promising zero-shot generalization to RWP-636 and AIM-500. Moreover, X-Matte achieves up to a 9.4x inference speedup over a constructed single-step latent counterpart at high resolution, demonstrating the effectiveness of VAE-free pixel-space modeling for accurate and efficient image matting.

title: Dirichlet eigenvalues of Laplacian with potential on general graphs and Weyl limits in integer lattice spaces $Z^d$
authors: Huyuan Chen, Lixun Jia
abstract: In this paper, we first establish the existence of weighted Dirichlet eigenvalues of the Laplacian with a vertex weight on an infinite, connected and locally finite graph, via building compact embeddings of suitable spaces, when the weight decays faster at infinity than the optimal Hardy weight. In the particular integer lattice space $Z^d$, we apply a segmentation technique to estimate the mean Riesz potential over the entire space, thereby deriving estimates for the eigenvalue counting function and establishing the Weyl limit of the eigenvalues.

title: Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Yuze Lu
abstract: When the lead robot cannot continue, what should it send the teammate that must finish the route? We replay a frozen receiver at each contact under alternative messages. Across 3,920 autonomous departures in 106 environments, adding the view before the lead's last action block to its executed actions raised success by 7.51 percentage points (pp) per RxR handoff and 8.54 pp per SAGE handoff. Per departure the gains were 2.23 and 1.44 pp, respectively. The lead continuing in simulation defines the empirical full-history ceiling (Solo). At contact, the lead had accumulated a median of 41 frames. Sending one frame when available recovered 24% of the full-history advantage over actions alone in SAGE and 30% in RxR. Over an estimated progress cue in SAGE, the image rescued 100 routes and reversed 54 successes. Near-goal receivers finished outside less often (63.1% to 51.7%, post hoc). In secondary comparisons the earlier view outperformed the contact view by 6-7 pp per handoff. Exact-route specificity and image gains at controlled starts with mostly unknown progress or outside the goal region remained unresolved. Gains were detectable from about 7 kB per handoff. Random transmission matched within size bins nearly equaled the learned sender's team success. At a required handoff, a view of the approach to the last maneuver helps the receiver finish.

title: MuSTRNG: A Muon-Based Synchronizable True Random Number Generation System
authors: Bohang Zou, Shubin Liu, Yu Wang, Ting Wang, Changqing Feng, Zhongtao Shen
abstract: Cosmic-ray muons provide naturally occurring stochastic events detectable by spatially separated devices, offering a potential physical source for synchronized random-bit generation. This is possible because the same physical muons can be independently detected by both devices and used to derive corresponding random-bit segments. Therefore, identifying common muon events and correctly aligning the event sequences are essential for synchronized random-bit generation. This article presents MuSTRNG, a muon-based synchronizable true random number generation system with two synchronization methods: Tracking--Tracking and Tracking--Nontracking. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, track-based screening removes events whose reconstructed tracks do not intersect the detector area of the other device; angle-based screening partitions reconstructed directions into angular bins and aligns the event sequences to remove inconsistent pairs; and timestamp-based screening compares higher-order timestamp bits to further suppress residual mismatches. Tracking--Nontracking synchronization applies track-based screening only at the tracking-capable device, followed by timestamp-based screening between the two devices. A prototype with two tracking-capable devices was evaluated. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, the three-stage process reduced the invalid-event ratio to 0.28% using 15-bit random segments, while the generated bit sequences showed generally favorable results in the applicable NIST SP~800-22 tests. Reprocessing the data without track information from one device provided preliminary support for Tracking--Nontracking synchronization, yielding an invalid-event ratio of 0.30% using 5-bit random segments. These results demonstrate the feasibility of muon-based synchronized random-bit generation under different device configurations, with potential application to secure communications.

title: OmniMeld: Enhancing Audio-Visual Understanding via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Daili Hua, Yifan Dai, Bohan Zeng, Yuran Wang, Zihao Wu, Chengzhuo Tong, Guoqing Jiang, Liwei Chen, Zhiheng Qin, Xuanping Li, Wentao Zhang
abstract: Audio-visual understanding requires perceptual grounding, temporal understanding, and semantic inference. Multi-teacher distillation can consolidate these capabilities, but direct probability matching does not explicitly capture teacher prediction changes across audio-visual conditions. We introduce OmniMeld, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that integrates domain expertise through modality-response-guided distribution matching. We train four teachers covering grounding and correspondence, temporal dynamics and event structure, causal and inferential reasoning, and contextual and holistic understanding. Each sample is routed to its corresponding teacher for supervision conditioned on student-generated answer prefixes. We derive transport costs from teacher prediction changes over shared candidate tokens across audio-visual conditions, using optimal transport to match student predictions to those of the teacher under complete audio-visual input. We also construct OmniMeld-20K for domain-specialized teacher training. The dataset spans four capability domains, with responses structured into evidence, reasoning, and answer sections and verified through consistency checks and media-based review. Experiments on audio-visual and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate competitive teacher performance among similarly sized open-source models. The student improves over its base model across all evaluated benchmarks and surpasses the teachers' base model on several benchmarks.

title: Structured Noise Diffusion for Echocardiography Haze Removal
authors: Zike Luo, Hao Li, Mengxiao Wang, Qingya Li, Ching-Hui Sia, Lei Li
abstract: Echocardiographic images are frequently degraded by spatially structured haze artifacts that obscure anatomical boundaries and hinder clinical analysis. Conventional diffusion models typically employ pixel-independent Gaussian noise, limiting their ability to represent localized ultrasound haze. In this study, we propose a structure-informed diffusion framework that explicitly models ultrasound haze as an accumulation of localized Gaussian components constrained by the ultrasound fan geometry. The forward process generates spatially correlated corruption by sampling component locations and scales, providing a formulation that better reflects the spatial characteristics of real echo artifacts. During reverse restoration, a dual-head network predicts an anchor probability map and Gaussian scale parameters to progressively remove structured artifacts while reducing the center bias associated with direct coordinate regression. We evaluated the framework on the public DehazingEcho2025 benchmark and two private clinical datasets, without retraining or fine-tuning on either private cohort. Our method achieved the highest mean generalized contrast-to-noise ratio across all three datasets, reaching $0.715 \pm 0.090$ on the public benchmark while preserving tissue edges.

title: A Global Solver for Minimum-Time Connectivity Restoration in UAV Networks
authors: Huan Lin, Lianghui Ding
abstract: Node failures can split an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) network into disconnected groups. Restoring communication requires moving the surviving aircraft, and the operator needs both an executable movement plan and an assessment of how much shorter the recovery could be. We develop Connectivity Restoration Branch-and-Bound (CR-BB), which returns a feasible plan and numerical displacement bounds; dividing these bounds by the common speed gives the corresponding time interval. Exact-arithmetic guarantees are established by the theorems. When the gap is not closed, the plan is feasible but not certified optimal. A fixed-tree subproblem is a second-order cone program. CR-BB searches over spanning trees and uses a Joint Mandatory-Link Bound (JMLB) to remove tree families that cannot improve the incumbent; Progress-based Adaptive Stopping (PAS) controls the search budget. On 200 matched cases, enabling the JMLB in the branch bound raised the number of cases meeting the prescribed displacement gap from 182 to 200 and reduced mean expanded nodes from 49.6 to 0.7. On a 60-case exact comparison, CR-BB met the gap in 90.0% of cases, compared with 55.0% for a spanning-tree mixed-integer conic formulation and 37.5% of the eight runs completed by an independent optimizer. On 1,000 paired recovery cases, CR-BB planned first restored connectivity in 72.35 steps on average, compared with 124.32 for an edge-augmentation baseline with conic refinement, a 41.8% reduction; on the common 50% subset the reduction was 28.1%. Across 2,466 cases, PAS reduced cumulative solver time by 20.9% and expanded nodes by 31.1% relative to a fixed search budget, with a 0.36-step mean increase in planned steps; most of the saving came from cases where neither configuration met the gap, and 60 plans became longer.

title: PRISM: Perceptual Rate-Controllable Extreme Image Compression with Visual State-Space Models
authors: Md Adnan Faisal Hossain, Fengqing Zhu
abstract: Generative codecs built on pretrained diffusion priors achieve high perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates (below 0.05 bpp). However, most methods still require a separate model for each bitrate, and offer no control over the amount of detail synthesized. Their rate efficiency also depends on the entropy model, where Mamba-based state-space models (SSMs) have recently improved autoregressive context modeling. However, conventional SSM scans are not aligned with the decoding order, and each decoding pass restarts from an empty state, discarding context accumulated in previous passes. We propose PRISM, an extreme image compression method that addresses these limitations. A single model provides two continuous controls: a rate knob that traverses the rate-distortion curve and a realism knob that adjusts the level of detail synthesized. Its visual state-space (VSS) context model introduces a decode-order-aligned (DOA) scan, which predicts each latent from a state that summarizes all decoded context, and cross-tap state carry, which initializes each tap with a summary of the previous one. Experiments show that PRISM outperforms both variable-rate and fixed-rate codecs, requiring on average 22% less bitrate than the strongest baseline at equal FID while also achieving higher PSNR.

title: Higher-Dimensional Automata in Geometric Logic
authors: Kenan Oggad
abstract: What does the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton know about its infinite behaviour that its language does not? We write partial HDAs with an infinite run as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory with no choice. The topos of a machine is that of sheaves on its prefixes. The label word of a prefix records the shape and acceptance bit of each cell with the ipomset of each step. Under unique choice these words give a geometric morphism to the label topos of sheaves on label words, which thus records the shapes and acceptance bits that the Büchi language forgets. Machines sharing their Büchi language and their frames can differ over the label topos. The bouquet of two squares shares its frame and its Büchi language with the interleaved square; each accepted run of either reads the two events in parallel forever. Only the interleaved square has runs through cells of shape a, and the geometric sequent excluding such runs separates the two over the label topos. Over alphabets with decidable equality, finite rigid machines are unambiguous exactly when their label maps are inclusions of locales, and their equivalence over the label topos is decided whenever either is unambiguous. Equivalences of frames over the label topos transport points with their labels, and the invariants of fibres and of the language of points follow from this transport. On finite partial HDAs over alphabets with decidable equality, Muller and Büchi acceptance coincide exactly under a weak form of excluded middle.

title: Geometry Sets the Neutral MLIP-DFT Gap in Non-Covalent Binding, and Charged Systems Fail
authors: Rui Ding, Zixin Ding, Rodrigo Pires Ferreira, Diantong Li, Junhong Chen, Yuxin Chen
abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are widely expected to substitute for explicit quantum chemistry when screening molecular interactions. On non-covalent binding we find that this expectation holds for neutral chemistry and fails for charged chemistry. We audit the FAIRChem UMA OMol head, without task-specific fine-tuning, on 5,567 probe-target dimers from 18 benchmarks across nine fidelity arms, using RAPIDS (Rapid Atomistic Probe-target Interaction Discovery Scaffold), a training-free inference-time scaffold. First, on neutral chemistry RAPIDS reaches a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.37 kcal/mol, matching or beating every explicit DFT single-point fidelity (1.42-1.50 kcal/mol), so the remaining MLIP-DFT gap is geometric rather than a learned-surface error. Second, charged systems form a qualitatively different regime: MAE jumps to 8.5-22.9 kcal/mol across three charged benchmarks; DFT single-point rescoring does not restore accuracy, geometry reoptimization restores it for ionic hydrogen bonds and ion-molecule dimers, and the failure persists across all three MLIP backbones. Third, the residual failures are structured: signed biases cluster by chemistry family, and whether a fidelity fails catastrophically transfers across families more reliably than error magnitude, enabling cost-aware fidelity selection. RAPIDS-Select, a closed-form rule on cheap precomputed features, uses about 37% less compute than a strong static DFT baseline at matched accuracy, and on a newly computed charged benchmark cuts the catastrophe rate from 68% to 5.7%. On WetSenseBench, a wet-lab-grounded host-guest selectivity benchmark from eight sensing studies, RAPIDS without DFT follow-up recovers 82.9% pair-level agreement on the seven studies above its ~1 kcal/mol precision floor.

title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
authors: Peihang Lin, Shanmei Wanyan, Mucheng Zhu, Ying Jiang, Chris H. Rycroft, Chenfanfu Jiang, Jiayin Lu
abstract: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.

title: Learning a Whole-Body Pivot-Walking Gait for Heavy-Box Transport with a Humanoid
authors: Rikuto Hidaka, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
abstract: Through pivot walking, humans can transport objects that are too heavy to lift. Previous humanoid studies have relied on planned sequences in which object manipulation and stepping are executed separately and the object is brought to rest between successive rotations. However, few studies have developed a single learned controller for humanoid pivot walking. In this paper, we propose a single reinforcement-learning policy that jointly coordinates stepping, balance control, and object manipulation. The policy is trained using rewards that promote alternating pivot motions and a phase reference that progresses according to the displacement of the object. In simulation, we confirmed that the humanoid can pivot a box. For deployment, we fine-tuned the policy into an object-blind version that follows a periodic clock instead of the progress reference. On the real robot, the deployed policy transported the box forward by more than 1 m in all five trials; each trial ended at a base-tilt safety stop. These results demonstrate that coordinated humanoid pivot walking can be learned with reinforcement learning and transferred to a physical humanoid robot without direct object-state sensing.

title: MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yixiao He, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Jiayu Wang, Ying Wei
abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models
authors: Yue Yu, Cong Zhang, David Crandall, Guanyu Hu
abstract: Roster construction is a critical decision problem in professional basketball, requiring teams to balance player quality, player complementarity, and financial constraints under uncertainty. Existing roster optimization models primarily rely on individual player ratings and aggregate performance statistics, which provide limited information about how players' offensive contributions vary with their teammates. Recent advances in player-tracking technology have enabled statistical analyses of spatial shooting patterns, but these insights have rarely informed roster construction. We bridge this gap by developing a data-driven, risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization framework for NBA roster construction. We first develop a Bayesian modeling framework that combines player statistics and spatial shot-chart data to identify player roles and estimate how teammate composition influences shot selection, shooting frequency, and scoring efficiency. The resulting model provides uncertainty-quantified offensive values for hypothetical five-player lineups, including combinations that have never played together. We then formulate roster construction as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that optimizes player acquisitions under NBA salary-cap regulations while allowing lineup playing-time allocations to adapt to uncertain player roles. We evaluate the framework using 240 team-offseason decisions over eight seasons and two additional held-out seasons. The results demonstrate that incorporating spatial shooting compatibility substantially changes optimal roster decisions and improves predicted offensive performance relative to approaches based on individual player values. We further find that flexibility in allocating playing time across lineups absorbs much of the uncertainty about player roles.

title: MMotion: Collaborative Cross-Scale Memory for Text-to-Motion Generation
authors: Zhaoxin Fan, Qingchen Yu, Kejian Wu, Jian Yang, Zeming Liu, wenjun wu, Lili Wang
abstract: Text-to-motion generation aims to synthesize realistic human motions from natural-language descriptions, enabling applications in animation, virtual avatars, and embodied agents. Despite recent progress, existing methods either retrieve motion exemplars or retain long-range context, but rarely exploit memory to jointly reason about semantics, dynamics, and generation history. In this paper, we propose MMotion, a collaborative multi-scale memory framework that unifies scale-conditioned semantic retrieval, latent dynamics modeling, and causal working memory. Specifically, semantic memory provides motion priors at different generation scales, dynamics memory captures latent state transitions, and working memory preserves causal context from previously generated motions. A collaborative fusion mechanism integrates these complementary memories to determine what motion to generate, how it should evolve, and how it should remain consistent with its history. MMotion is architecture-agnostic and can be readily integrated into both diffusion-based and next scale autoregressive models. Extensive experiments across standard benchmarks and diverse backbones demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines.

title: Spectral Optimal Transport for Dynamics-Aware Sign Language Generation
authors: Nabeela Khan, Bowen Wu, Runwu Shi, Hanlong Li, Benjamin Yen, Carlos Toshinori Ishi, Kazuhiro Nakadai
abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this issue, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Spin-vibronic order in Ba$_2$MgReO$_6$
authors: Zhishuo Huang, Takumi Gengo, Teruki Matsuzaki, Liviu F. Chibotaru, Naoya Iwahara
abstract: Strong spin-orbit coupling in $5d$ ions produces multipolar orders that conventional probes barely detect. In cubic $5d^1$ double perovskites, the spin-orbit quartet couples to Jahn-Teller vibrations, and resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) has established the resulting spin-orbit-lattice entangled (vibronic) states [Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{133}, 036501 (2024)]. We proposed that these vibronic states order cooperatively and thereby explain the hidden quadrupole and canted magnetic phases of Ba$_2$MgReO$_6$ [Phys. Rev. B \textbf{107}, L220404 (2023)], but that proposal rested on a simplified model. Here, we show that a spin-vibronic Hamiltonian derived from first principles, with a single scale factor for the elastic coupling, reproduces the ordered phases of Ba$_2$MgReO$_6$ with the same vibronic states that describe its RIXS spectra. With this factor bringing the quadrupolar transition to 34.7 K, near the measured 33 K, the theory predicts the magnetic transition at 19.3 K, against the measured 18 K, and reproduces the antiferro distortion and the ferro elongation between the transitions. These results support spin-vibronic order in Ba$_2$MgReO$_6$ and point to it as the origin of the hidden multipolar phases of $5d^1$ double perovskites.

title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
authors: Xiaoyang Lv, Peixin Wang, Jianhao Bai, Bai Xue, Min Zhang, Luke Ong
abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

title: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Inverse Design
authors: Antonia Panescu, Xin Wang, Haoran Xu, Qingyu Chen, Carlos Oliver, Rex Ying
abstract: RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into specified target structures. Existing methods rely on learned generators that can miss exact structural matches, especially beyond their training distributions, or on costly search over a vast, multimodal sequence space. Search is further complicated by globally coupled nucleotide interactions, as correcting one pairing error can create new errors beyond a fixed repair scope. To address this, we introduce KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that learns from verifier feedback to refine sequences for exact fold-back matching. Starting from candidates generated for a target secondary structure, KnitNet uses mismatched folds to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns to predict which edits are promising. This makes search progressively more informed and compute-efficient. Crucially, KnitNet generalizes across RNA structural regimes by changing only the optimization signal to match the verifier required by each setting. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, KnitNet increases exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve. On OpenKnot57 specifically, KnitNet is the first method to achieve exact computational matches for all complex, pseudoknotted structures. Beyond 2D, KnitNet improves 3D structural self-consistency over per-target RL by 7.8% while being 39.3% faster, demonstrating generalization and effective inference-time scaling across RNA design regimes.

title: Non-Existence of Eigenvalues and Interface States for the Schrödinger Operator with Longitudinal Interface Potentials
authors: Tomáš Dohnal, Anton Lochmann
abstract: We consider the Schrödinger operator in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a flat interface separating two half-spaces in which the real potential varies only in the directions parallel to the interface. This problem generally possesses no shift invariance. Nevertheless, using the method of multipliers, we prove the absence of eigenvalues. In addition, in the case of periodic potentials on each side of the interface the same method shows the absence of interface states which are quasi-periodic in the directions parallel to the interface and localized in the transverse direction.

title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding
authors: Yuxia Zhu, Shiying Zhang, Lingzhuang Sun, Song Yang, Siheng Wu, Xinglong Xu, Sizhe Qiu, Hao Liang, Cheng Tan, Asher Qin, Wentao Zhang
abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
authors: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan
abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.

title: Experimental Quantum Hardware Benchmarks of Flat Non-Clifford Hypergraph States, Antipodal Obstructions, and Nonlocal Games on IBM Heron r2
authors: Filipe Martins Vono, Valéria Gonzaga Santos, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo
abstract: Real-hardware demonstrations of quantum contextuality have reached high precision on superconducting processors, exemplified by Google Quantum AI's Mermin-Peres magic square and stabilizer games on Willow (Science, 2026). Extending such benchmarks beyond the Clifford regime requires non-Clifford hypergraph states |ψ_f> = 2^{-n/2} \sum_x (-1)^{f(x)} |x> governed by discrete algebraic invariants. Building on our Lean 4-verified framework of Modular Walsh Rigidity and Antipodal Obstructions, we present an experimental study on two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_fez, ibm_kingston) across 3 to 50 qubits and 11 auditable jobs (2.13 RUs total). First, we verify antipodal obstructions and mod-17 Walsh rigidity for degree-3/4 states (n=6,8,10), observing 5.4x-11.6x X-basis flatness separation between bent states, obstructed controls, and a degree-4 mod-3 fooler (W = +-1 mod 3), plus n=7 nonlinearity extraction (54.83 vs. 56.00). Second, barrier-protected Loschmidt echoes confirm non-Clifford coherence up to genuinely entangled 16-qubit degree-4 states (1,488x above random on ibm_fez; 17,296x on ibm_kingston for 2x8q, a 2.87x cross-chip gain) and locate a Heavy-Hex depth-513 coherence cliff. Third, calibration-aware layout raises the raw Mermin-Peres win rate on ibm_fez to 96.85 +- 0.09% raw (+87.4 sigma above 88.89% classical; 1.45 pp below Willow's 98.30% raw), while a tensored SPAM diagnostic reaches 98.35%. Uniformly random even-weight GHZ parity games beat the classical bound up to n=30 (89.44% [+79.4 sigma] at 6q to 59.46 +- 0.54% [+17.4 sigma] at 30q). Finally, 3-qubit CCZ rotated Mermin-3 (83.95 +- 0.29%, +31.2 sigma) and Hardy/Guhne-Cabello (77.15 +- 0.33%, +6.5 sigma) games strictly violate the exhaustive 75.00% LHV ceiling, and degree-3/4 antipodal parity witnesses achieve up to +45.87 pp (n=12) and +35.79 pp joint advantage on connected 16-qubit degree-4 states.

title: Slow mixing of Gibbs sampling for the quantum Curie-Weiss model
authors: Xiaoyang Huang
abstract: Hamiltonian evolution can spread local operators across a dense quantum magnet. We show that this global support does not remove the bottleneck to thermalization in the quantum Curie-Weiss model: at fixed low temperature and weak transverse field, the Chen-Kastoryano-Gilyen Gibbs sampler [arXiv: 2311.09207] has an exponentially large mixing-time lower bound. A dynamical quantum bottleneck theory that generalizes the classical notion of conductance has been proposed alongside existing frameworks that rely on spatial locality. We also give a complementary interpretation of slow mixing using an effective Fokker-Planck equation.

title: Electrostatic effects on settling cloud droplets: from pair collisions to size distribution evolution
authors: Pijush Patra, John S. Wettlaufer
abstract: We investigate how droplet charge and a uniform vertical electric field influence collisions between cloud droplets settling in still air and how these collisions shape the droplet size distribution. We compute collision efficiencies by analyzing the relative trajectories of pairs of spherical, conducting droplets, accounting for droplet inertia, exact hydrodynamic, electrostatic, and van der Waals forces. The hydrodynamic interactions are based on exact two-body solutions for Stokes flow with interfacial mobility and internal circulation. In the absence of an applied electric field, collisions between like-charged droplets are suppressed, whereas collisions between oppositely-charged droplets are enhanced. A vertical electric field promotes collisions between uncharged droplets through induced polarization and, when sufficiently strong, can overcome the repulsion between like-charged droplets. When the larger droplet has a radius of $10$ or $20μ$m raising the electric field strength from $5\times10^{4}$ to $3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ can enhance the collision efficiency of uncharged droplet pairs by an order of magnitude. Depending on droplet size and field strength, for oppositely charged pairs, an applied electric field can either enhance or suppress collisions relative to the zero-field case. Using collision kernels computed from droplet pair trajectories, we solve the stochastic collection equation with a flux method on a two-dimensional grid that resolves droplet mass and charge. For an initial mean droplet radius of $10μ$m , by $40$ min in every electrified case the large-droplet mode of the mass spectrum reaches a larger radius than in the hydrodynamic reference case. This suggests that electrostatic interactions can hasten warm rain initiation by accelerating droplet growth through collision and coalescence.

title: The asymptotic spectrum of tensors is connected
authors: Péter Vrana, Jeroen Zuiddam
abstract: We prove path-connectedness of the asymptotic spectrum of complex tensors of every fixed order $k \geq 3$: every spectral point is connected by a path to every "one leg versus the rest" flattening rank. In particular, the asymptotic spectrum evaluated at any fixed tensor is a closed interval, answering a question of Strassen. This was previously known only on specific families of tensors (Strassen, FOCS 1986, Crelle 1987-1991; Wigderson and Zuiddam, Bull. AMS 2026) or for specific families of spectral points (Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam, STOC 2018; Sakabe, Doğan and Walter, FOCS 2026; Alman, Li and Pratt, FOCS 2026). To obtain our path-connectedness theorem we develop a general method for "interpolating" between spectral points, which applies to Strassen semirings that are appropriately decomposable (in the sense of an information-theoretic "method of types" on the semiring) and whose spectral points satisfy a cover property (inspired by slice rank). This covers tensors and asymptotic rank (with "types" given by decomposition into symmetric group irreps), as well as other objects and asymptotic problems, like graphs and Shannon capacity, where it matches the interpolation of Vrana (2019). Using our interpolation methods we furthermore obtain new results and simpler proofs of previous results regarding the asymptotic spectrum of rectangular matrix multiplication, polynomial multiplication and non-crossing (laminar) quantum functionals.

title: Multi-Party Authorization of Maintenance Prescriptions on a Permissioned Blockchain
authors: Siyuan Chen, Ebru Turanoglu Bekar, Anders Skoogh
abstract: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, an equipment supplier's model may recommend an intervention that a plant schedules, a contractor executes, and a quality or safety function approves. A shared ledger records who submitted the prescription, yet cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule produced it. We require permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that calculation before releasing a work order. On a four-organization Hyperledger Fabric testbed using a public engine benchmark, this stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, whereas hash checks accepted four that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.

title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit
authors: Nicole Ellenbach, Juliane C. Wilcke, Maurizio Morelli, Elisa Noltenius, Simona Jell, Sebastian Kobold, Carolin Herrmann, Anne-Laure Boulesteix
abstract: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

title: A formula to construct all elements of finite order in Riordan matrix groups
authors: Irina Arévalo, Ismael Gómez García, Ana Luzón, M. M. Martínez-Rico, L. F. Prieto-Martínez
abstract: We characterize the elements of finite order in the Riordan group over the complex field by providing explicit conditions on their entries. Our main result generalizes a previous characterization of involutions to arbitrary finite orders and gives a constructive procedure to determine all Riordan matrices of a prescribed finite order from a suitable choice of parameters. The proof relies on an inductive analysis of the principal submatrices. We further derive consequences for the Lagrange subgroup and the group of formal power series under composition, obtaining a characterization of finite-order series and a constructive description of the solutions to associated functional equations.

title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification
authors: Diego Carrascosa, Tristan Pank, Qudus Onikeku, Mas'ud Onikeku, Jeremy A Frusco, Osubi Craig, Angelos Barmpoutis
abstract: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.
